transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I came in because… I’m having a hard time with something that keeps happening, and it’s starting to make it impossible to function at work. I keep hearing people talking about me — like through the conference room walls, or sometimes from my phone even when I know it’s off. It’s usually board members or staff, and they’re saying things like I’m ruining the company, that I’m making terrible decisions, that everyone knows it.

And it’s not like a vague thought or me just worrying. It sounds clear, like real voices, like they’re right there. Sometimes I’ll answer out loud before I realize no one else heard anything, and then I feel… embarrassed, or scared, because I can’t tell in the moment why it’s so obvious to me and not to anyone else. That’s why I’m here.
Have you noticed any periods where, along with hearing these voices, you also felt unusually sad, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually energetic, elated, or irritable for days at a time?

I don’t… I don’t know that I’d describe it that way. I mean, I get upset because of the voices, obviously. It’s hard not to feel shaken or worn down when you keep hearing people criticize you like that. But I’m not sure if that’s the same as being unusually sad or hopeless for days, like out of nowhere.

And the energetic or elated thing… no, I don’t think so. I have days where I’m tense and kind of wired because I’m trying to keep up appearances and keep everything under control, but it doesn’t feel like I’m euphoric or suddenly full of amazing energy. Irritable, maybe in the sense that I’m on edge, but again, it feels connected to what’s happening, not like a separate mood episode or whatever.

I guess what I’m trying to say is, I haven’t really noticed a distinct period where my mood completely changes for days at a time. It’s more that the voices happen, and then I react to them.

Do you have any medical conditions, recent illnesses, head injuries, or use of substances (including prescription medications, alcohol, or recreational drugs) that started around the same time these voices began?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, nothing is jumping out at me as, “Oh, that started and then the voices started.” I haven’t had, like… some obvious accident or illness that I can point to and say it explains it.

As far as substances, I don’t really know what would count as “around the same time” in the way you mean. I’m not trying to dodge the question — I just don’t have a clear answer where something changed and then all of this began. I haven’t noticed a connection like that.

If you mean prescriptions or alcohol or anything like that, I can try to think it through more carefully, but there isn’t some big new thing that stands out to me right now. It feels more like this just… started happening, and then kept happening, and I’ve been trying to manage it.
How long have you been experiencing these voices - has it been less than a month, a few months, or longer than six months?

It’s been… about three months, I think. Not just a couple of days or a week. I remember at first I kept trying to explain it away, like maybe I was overhearing something through the wall or my phone had somehow not turned off properly, but then it kept happening.

So, yes — a few months. Around three months that I’ve been hearing the voices from the walls or from my phone. It feels longer because it’s been so exhausting, but if I’m trying to be accurate, I’d say about the past three months.

Besides hearing these voices, have others told you that your speech or thinking seems disorganized or hard to follow, or have you noticed a decline in your motivation, hygiene, or ability to express emotions?

I don’t think people say my speech is disorganized exactly… I mean, maybe they look confused sometimes, but I’m not sure if that’s because I’m not explaining things well or because I’m trying to explain too much at once. I used to be very clear, very quick. At work especially, I was the person driving every idea, keeping the room moving, calling people after openings, following up on every detail.

Now it’s like… I can sit at my desk for hours just staring at the agenda. I’ll have the papers right in front of me, and I know I’m supposed to make decisions, send emails, talk to staff, and I just don’t. It’s not even that I’m making a choice not to — it feels like there’s nothing there to push me forward.

And at home, I barely speak to my husband sometimes. Not because I’m angry with him. I just… don’t have much to say, or it feels like too much effort to form it. Same with staff. I’ll sit through meetings and say almost nothing, which is not like me at all.

The hardest part is I used to really love my work. It mattered to me. I could feel that excitement and urgency, and now I look at the same things and feel almost nothing. Like I’m watching someone else’s life from behind glass. So yes, I guess there has been a decline in motivation, and probably in how much emotion I show. I don’t like admitting that, but it’s true.

Thinking back, would you say this drop in motivation, energy, and emotional expression has been going on continuously for about six months or more, or did it really start only in the last few months alongside the voices?

No… if I’m being honest, it didn’t only start with the voices. The voices are newer — that’s the part that made everything feel impossible to ignore — but the drop in me, the energy and the drive and that feeling like I’m not fully present… that’s been building for much longer.

I think it goes back about two years and four months, around when the company expanded and I was put in charge of the new arts-and-commerce division. At the time, I told myself it was just the workload, the pressure, the responsibility of proving the whole thing could work. And I did keep functioning for a while, or at least I looked like I was functioning. I could still show up, make decisions, sit in meetings, be the executive version of myself.

But looking back, that was when something started changing. I had to push harder for things that used to come naturally. I stopped feeling that spark about the work, even though it was supposed to be exactly the kind of challenge I would’ve loved. It wasn’t sudden, like one day I woke up different. It was more like… little by little, I became less myself.

So yes, it’s definitely been more than six months. More like a little over two years — about two years and four months — since that expansion and the new division happened. The voices came later, but the decline had already been happening before that.

latest_inference.note: The chronic (2+ year) decline in motivation, emotional expression, and social engagement preceding the psychotic symptoms indicates a schizophrenic prodrome rather than an isolated delusional disorder (F22) or a brief/organic psychosis (F06.2). No evidence of medical, substance, or mood-episode etiology was found, further ruling out F06.2 and mood-related psychosis. The combination of negative symptoms and persistent auditory hallucinations over 3+ months supports schizophrenia as the primary diagnosis.

She explicitly denies any distinct manic or depressive mood episode overlapping with the psychotic symptoms, ruling out schizoaffective disorder or a mood disorder with psychotic features. No temporal association with substances, medications, or medical/neurological illness was identified, excluding substance-induced or secondary psychosis. The combination of positive symptoms (hallucinations) and prominent negative symptoms (avolition, blunted affect, alogia) persisting well beyond 6 months, with clear functional impairment and no mood or organic etiology, supports a diagnosis of Schizophrenia (F20.9).
